context: Bridget, a South African shopper, wants to buy an iPod priced in pounds (£) and pays in rand (R). The rand cost is the price in pounds multiplied by the exchange rate, the number of rand in £1. She compares the rand cost at the current exchange rate with the rand cost after the rate has dropped.
stem: Bridget wants to buy an iPod that costs $\text{£ }{=p}$, with the exchange rate currently at $\text{£1}=\text{R}{=r1}$. In a month the exchange rate drops to $\text{£1}=\text{R}{=r2}$. How much will she save, in rand, if she buys the iPod at the new rate instead of at the current rate?
solution: The cost in rand is the price in pounds multiplied by the exchange rate.
The rate has dropped, so the iPod now costs less and the difference is a saving: $\text{Saving}=\text{R}{=c1}-\text{R}{=c2}=\text{R}{=saving}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Subtracts the rates but never multiplies by the price in pounds
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student finds how far the exchange rate moved (old rate minus new rate) and gives that as the saving or loss, forgetting that the item costs many pounds and each pound is affected by the change.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Gives the rand cost at the new rate as the saving or loss
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student computes the price in rand at the new rate and stops there, instead of subtracting it from (or taking it away from) the rand cost at the old rate to find the difference.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Divides the pound price by the exchange rate
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student converts pounds to rand by dividing the price in pounds by the number of rand per pound instead of multiplying, so the rand costs and the saving come out wrong.

notes: Basic entry point of the skill, modelled on ex9-6-1b (Bridget's iPod, saving when the rate drops). Strips the book's extra 'she estimates' sentence so the learner meets only the two rates: rand cost at the current rate, rand cost at the lower rate, subtract. Direction is always a drop, so the answer is a positive saving. Ranges: price 20 to 150 pounds in steps of 5, current rate R10 to R20, new rate 1 to 6 below it and never under R7 (the book's rates run R9 to R20). Saving is a whole number between 20 and 900 rand. Wording 'compared with buying at the current rate' is explicit so a blind solver cannot read the saving against any other rate. A numeric family has no distractors, so the proposed misconceptions describe the wrong numbers a marker might see (r1 - r2, p * r2, p / r1 - p / r2). Standard (the book's own three-rate exercises) and advanced tiers were not requested; the book has no exercise harder than a single comparison, so no advanced family was written.
